newsitem.title: UK: Irish economy thrives but concerns seen ahead.
newsitem.headline: Irish economy thrives but concerns seen ahead.

text.p: Irish government bonds have been thriving amid economic restructuring and enthusiasm for a single European currency, but investors must not get complacent, analysts said on Friday.
The country was rewarded for its economic turnaround on Thursday when Moody's Investors Service raised its rating for Irish bond and bank deposits to Aa1 from Aa2.
But the link between sterling and the punt, and uncertainty over Britain's attitude towards European economic and monetary union (EMU), will cast shadows over the debt market.

"Both the background to the Irish economy and fact that we have uncertainty due to the link in with sterling, will mean spreads will remain relatively high versus Germany and the Irish bond market will be outperformed by hard core Europe at least for the time being," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at BankAmerica in London.
He said the 10-year Irish bond yield spread against German Bunds was currently around 85 basis points (0.85 percentage points) and would probably move out towards 100 basis points.
Analysts said sterling strength was pulling the punt higher, and could damage Ireland's chances of qualifying for the first wave of EMU, planned for 1999.
The punt is currently in a 15 percent fluctuation band within the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
Hawkins said authorities might want to push the punt down to within a 6.0 percent band initially, then aim for 2.25 percent.
In order to achieve this, Hawkins said an interest rate cut would probably be needed, but was not justified by the domestic fundamentals, given buoyant consumer spending.
Such a move would lead to some steepening of the yield curve in the short term, he added.

Paul Horne, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris, said he was not overly concerned about sterling strength. He expected the currency to rise further but fall sharply in the second half of the year, taking the punt with it.
What was more of a concern was the attitude of a future British government towards participation in EMU, Horne said. Elections have to take place in Britain by May.
